contradictions.question: Is it okay to ask for things while praying?
contradictions.summary: The contradiction targets the question of importunity — persistent, repetitive petitioning in prayer. Matthew 6:7-8 directly condemns it, with Jesus telling the disciples not to babble like the Gentiles because the Father already knows what they need. The cited proof-text for the opposing view, Luke 8:5,7, is the Parable of the Sower and has nothing to do with prayer. The actual SAB proof-texts for importunity are Luke 11:5-13 (the friend at midnight) and Luke 18:1-8 (the persistent widow), where Jesus explicitly teaches that persistence in asking is rewarded.
contradictions.commentary: The substantive contradiction here is real and well-attested in Synoptic scholarship — Matthew 6:7-8 directly contradicts the importunity teachings in Luke 11 and Luke 18. In Matthew's Sermon on the Mount, Jesus instructs disciples not to heap up empty phrases (battalogeo) like the Gentiles, because the Father already knows what they need before they ask. The whole point of the Lord's Prayer that follows is brevity. Luke, meanwhile, frames Jesus' parables of the friend at midnight (11:5-13) and the persistent widow (18:1-8) around exactly the opposite logic — keep asking, keep knocking, wear God down like a widow harasses an unjust judge. Luke 18:1 explicitly states the parable's lesson: "that they ought always to pray, and not to faint." Apologists like Blomberg and Carson typically harmonize by claiming Matthew condemns only mindless pagan repetition while Luke commends sincere persistence, but this is a distinction without a textual basis — both passages address the question of whether God responds to repeated, persistent asking, and they answer it differently. The deeper source-critical point is that Matthew and Luke are deploying Jesus tradition to make competing rhetorical points about prayer's mechanics. The contradiction is real; the cited verses in this entry are not the ones that establish it. Luke 8:5,7 belongs to the Parable of the Sower and has zero connection to the prayer question. This appears to be a scrape error where the wrong verse range got attached to the entry.

contradictions.question: Why was the Sabbath instituted?
contradictions.summary: The two versions of the Decalogue give incompatible etiologies for the Sabbath. Exodus 20:11 grounds it in creation — Yahweh rested on the seventh day after making the heavens and earth, and Israel is commanded to keep the Sabbath because God did. Deuteronomy 5:15 grounds it in the Exodus — Israel is to keep the Sabbath because Yahweh brought them out of Egypt with a mighty hand. These are not complementary motives; they are two distinct theological rationales for the same commandment, each presented as the reason God commanded it.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the cleanest source-critical fingerprints in the entire Pentateuch. The Priestly redactor of Exodus 20:11 reaches back to Genesis 2:2-3 — also a Priestly text — and grounds the Sabbath in the cosmic rest of God after creation. The Deuteronomist (singular hand or school, traditional D source) has no interest in that creation theology. The Deuteronomic Sabbath is humanitarian and historical — you rest, your slaves rest, your animals rest, because you used to be slaves yourselves. Two rationales, two source streams, one commandment. Apologists like Gleason Archer typically harmonize by claiming both reasons are true and complementary, that God can have multiple motives for a single commandment. That's true in the abstract, but it does not address the textual problem. Each Decalogue presents its rationale as *the* reason ("wherefore," "therefore the LORD thy God commanded thee"), and the rationales reflect distinct theological programs — P's cosmological Sabbath versus D's social-justice Sabbath. The Documentary Hypothesis predicts exactly this kind of doublet. Mark Smith and Jeffrey Tigay treat the divergence as a textbook case of the redactor's failure (or refusal) to harmonize competing traditions. The contradiction isn't a problem unless you assume a single human author writing a unified theology — which is precisely what historical-critical scholarship has not assumed for over a century.

contradictions.question: Should you be baptized?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 28:19 places baptism at the center of the risen Jesus' Great Commission to the eleven — go, make disciples, baptize them in the triune name. Paul in 1 Corinthians 1:14, 17 says the opposite about his own mission — he thanks God he baptized almost no one in Corinth, and flatly states that Christ did not send him to baptize but to preach the gospel. The contradiction is at the level of mission priority: Matthew's Jesus makes baptism constitutive of the commission; Paul explicitly excludes it from his own.
contradictions.commentary: The tension here is real but more nuanced than a flat yes/no contradiction. Matthew 28:19 is the climactic command of the Gospel — disciples are made by baptizing and teaching, in the triune name. Most critical scholars (Davies-Allison, Luz) treat 28:19 as a late, post-resurrection composition reflecting the practice of Matthew's community c. 80-90 CE, including the developed triune baptismal formula which is otherwise unattested in this form in the rest of the NT. Paul, writing earlier (mid-50s CE) and apparently unaware of any dominical baptismal command, treats baptism as ancillary to his apostolic calling. In 1 Corinthians 1:17 he draws a sharp distinction: "Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel." Apologists like Blomberg harmonize by noting that Paul baptized *some* (Crispus, Gaius, the household of Stephanas) and that his statement is hyperbolic emphasis on preaching, not rejection of the rite. Fair enough — but that harmonization assumes Paul knew of and accepted the Great Commission as a binding command, which the textual evidence doesn't support. If Paul had received a dominical instruction to baptize all nations, his rhetorical disavowal in 1 Corinthians 1:17 would be theologically suicidal. The more parsimonious reading is that the Great Commission in its Matthean form represents a later ecclesiastical development that Paul did not inherit. That is of course a subjective opinion on the evidence, but the evidence leans heavily in that direction.

contradictions.question: Is it okay to marry your brother's widow?
contradictions.summary: Deuteronomy 25:5 not only permits but commands a man to marry his deceased brother's childless widow — the institution of levirate marriage (Hebrew yibbum), with the explicit purpose of raising up offspring to perpetuate the dead brother's name. Leviticus 20:21 flatly prohibits exactly the same act, calling it an "unclean thing" (niddah) that uncovers the brother's nakedness, with the penalty that the couple shall be childless. Same action, opposite rulings.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the cleanest Pentateuchal legal contradictions in the entire corpus, and it's been recognized as such since the medieval rabbis. The Levitical prohibition (Holiness Code, H source) treats marriage to a brother's wife as incest — the same logic that prohibits a man from "uncovering the nakedness" of his father's wife or his daughter-in-law. The penalty in Leviticus 20:21 is even thematically barbed: the violators will be childless, which is precisely the opposite outcome from what Deuteronomy 25 commands the levirate to *prevent*. The Deuteronomic law (D source) addresses a different social anxiety entirely — preserving the dead man's lineage and inheritance line. Apologists like Archer and Walton harmonize by claiming Leviticus addresses marriage to a living brother's wife (adultery) while Deuteronomy addresses marriage to a deceased brother's widow. That harmonization is textually plausible for Leviticus 18:16 (which is parallel), but it strains Leviticus 20:21, which doesn't specify the brother's state. More importantly, the rabbinic tradition itself acknowledged the tension — m. Yebamot is one giant attempt to harmonize the laws, ultimately concluding that the Deuteronomic levirate *overrides* the Levitical prohibition only in the specific case of childless widowhood. That's not harmonization; that's legislative arbitration between two laws that conflict on their face. Source criticism explains this cleanly: H and D reflect distinct legal traditions with different priorities — H is preoccupied with priestly purity, D with social and economic preservation of the family line.

contradictions.question: Is it okay to hate your relatives?
contradictions.summary: Luke 14:26 has Jesus state baldly that no one can be his disciple without hating father, mother, wife, children, brothers, sisters, and his own life. Ephesians, by contrast, commands honoring father and mother as the first commandment with promise (6:2), commands husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church (5:25), and observes that no one ever hated his own flesh (5:29). The discipleship hatred Jesus demands is exactly what the Pauline household codes forbid.
contradictions.commentary: The standard apologist move on Luke 14:26 is to invoke the Semitic-idiom defense — the Greek miseo ("hate") functions as a Semitic comparative meaning "love less," and Matthew's parallel in 10:37 reads "he that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me," supposedly clarifying the meaning. That's a real linguistic phenomenon (cf. Genesis 29:31, Malachi 1:2-3 with Romans 9:13), and Joseph Fitzmyer and François Bovon both note it. But the apologist version oversells the case. Luke's wording is sharper than Matthew's, and Luke 14:26 lists "his own life also" — which complicates the simple "love less" reading, because the rest of the saying clearly requires costly self-renunciation, not just relative prioritization. The point of the radical wording is the *break* from natural family loyalty that itinerant discipleship demanded. Luke's Jesus is recruiting wandering charismatics who literally leave family behind, and the rhetoric matches the social practice. Ephesians, written by a later Pauline disciple (most critical scholars treat it as deutero-Pauline) c. 80-95 CE, reflects the second-generation church that had to figure out how to live in households and stay married — hence the Haustafel (household code) at 5:21-6:9 with its careful instructions about loving wives, honoring parents, and managing slaves. The trajectory from itinerant radicalism to settled household ethics is a well-documented sociological development in early Christianity (Theissen). The contradiction is real: the early Jesus tradition commands family-renunciation; the later household codes command family-affirmation.

contradictions.question: Should you obey your rulers?
contradictions.summary: Romans 13:1-6 commands universal submission to governing authorities on the grounds that they are ordained by God, are God's ministers, and punish only evildoers — resistance to them is resistance to God's ordinance and incurs damnation. Multiple narrative threads contradict this directly: the Hebrew midwives are blessed for disobeying Pharaoh (Exodus 1:17, 20), Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego defy Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 3:16-18), Daniel defies Darius (Daniel 6:7-10), and the New Testament itself describes righteous figures — Jesus, Daniel, the prophets — being executed or persecuted by the very rulers Romans 13 claims punish only the evil.
contradictions.commentary: Romans 13 is the single most theologically embarrassing passage in the Pauline corpus for any reader who has actually noticed how the Bible's own narratives treat rulers. Paul's claim is sweeping and grammatically unconditional — pasa psyche (every soul) is to be subject; there is no exception clause for unjust rulers. The text explicitly says rulers are not a terror to good works but to evil. That claim is empirically false within the biblical canon itself. The midwives obey God by lying to Pharaoh and are blessed for it. Daniel's friends face the fiery furnace for refusing imperial worship. Daniel himself prays in defiance of a royal decree. Acts 4:26-27 explicitly cites Psalm 2 against the rulers who conspired against Jesus. The cross itself is a state execution carried out by Pilate, a ruler Romans 13 would categorize as God's minister punishing evildoers. Apologists like Cranfield and Moo limit Romans 13 to legitimate authority acting within its proper sphere, importing a Lockean exception clause that Paul does not provide. Others (Käsemann, Wright) read Romans 13 against Paul's own apocalyptic framework — the present age is passing away (13:11-12), so submission is provisional and pragmatic, not absolute. Both readings are post-hoc attempts to soften a passage that, read at face value, commands the kind of obedience the Hebrew Bible's heroes are celebrated for refusing. The best critical assessment is that Paul, writing to a vulnerable Roman house-church in the late 50s, wanted to keep his communities off the imperial radar. The text reflects that pastoral situation rather than a universal theology — but Paul does not say that, and the Bible's own narratives consistently celebrate exactly the kind of civil disobedience Paul condemns.

contradictions.question: Do women have rights?
contradictions.summary: The contradiction sets the silencing-and-subordination passages — Genesis 3:16 (the husband rules over the wife as curse), 1 Timothy 2:12 (woman may not teach or have authority), 1 Corinthians 14:34 (women keep silence in the churches), 1 Peter 3:6 (Sarah as model of calling her husband lord) — against texts that show women exercising public religious and political authority: Deborah the prophetess judging Israel (Judges 4:4, 14-15; 5:7), the Joel/Acts 2:18 promise of women prophesying, and Philip's four daughters who prophesied (Acts 21:9). The same canon both denies women teaching authority and celebrates women exercising it.
contradictions.commentary: This is a real and recognized contradiction within the canon, and it sits at the heart of contemporary debates over women in ministry. The egalitarian/complementarian fight in evangelical scholarship (Payne, Belleville, Keener vs. Grudem, Schreiner) is fundamentally an attempt to reconcile these texts. The Pastorals (1-2 Timothy, Titus) and the disputed 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 passage are the silencing texts. Most critical scholars consider 1 Timothy pseudonymous, written c. 90-110 CE to address a more institutionalized church where the egalitarian impulse of earliest Christianity was being rolled back. Even more striking: 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 has serious textual problems. Gordon Fee argues it is a post-Pauline interpolation, noting that some Western manuscripts place these verses after 14:40 rather than after 14:33, which Fee takes as evidence of a marginal gloss that migrated into the text. Payne has extended this argument with manuscript evidence. If 14:34-35 is non-Pauline, then Paul's authentic position is reflected in 1 Corinthians 11, where women pray and prophesy in the assembly. The Deborah and Philip's-daughters texts are not isolated outliers — they reflect a real tradition of female prophetic and judicial authority in ancient Israel and the early church (cf. Phoebe the deacon in Romans 16:1, Junia the apostle in Romans 16:7, Priscilla teaching Apollos in Acts 18:26). The apologist harmonization typically restricts women's authority to extraordinary or domestic contexts while preserving male leadership in the institutional church. That harmonization works only by treating the silencing texts as normative and the agency texts as exceptional — a hermeneutical choice, not a textual one. Reverse the priority and the canon supports women's ministry; keep the priority and it forbids it. The contradiction is real, and the resolution is a question of which texts you privilege.

contradictions.question: Should you obey both God and your masters?
contradictions.summary: Colossians 3:22-23 and 1 Peter 2:18 command slaves to obey their earthly masters in all things, with fear and sincerity of heart, including "froward" (harsh) masters. Matthew 4:10 cites Deuteronomy that worship and service are owed to God alone. 1 Corinthians 7:23 tells believers, "Ye are bought with a price; be not ye the servants of men." Matthew 23:10 forbids anyone being called master (kathegetes) because Christ is the only master. The household codes' command to serve human masters with fear contradicts Jesus' and Paul's direct statements that service belongs to God alone.
contradictions.commentary: The household codes (Haustafeln) in Colossians 3:18-4:1, Ephesians 5:21-6:9, 1 Peter 2:13-3:7, and the Pastorals reflect the post-Pauline church's attempt to make Christianity socially respectable in the Greco-Roman world. The slave-master code in Colossians 3:22 and 1 Peter 2:18 is theologically jarring next to texts like 1 Corinthians 7:23 ("be not ye the servants of men") and Galatians 3:28 ("there is neither slave nor free"). Critical scholarship generally treats Colossians as deutero-Pauline and 1 Peter as pseudonymous, with the Haustafeln representing a second-generation Christian accommodation to Roman social norms. The contradiction with Jesus' teaching in Matthew 23:8-10 — "call no man your father upon the earth... neither be ye called masters" — is sharp. Jesus there forbids the very titles of hierarchical authority that the household codes inscribe. Apologists harmonize by distinguishing categories: slaves obey masters in a limited social sphere; ultimate worship and allegiance go to God alone; therefore there is no conflict. That distinction works rhetorically but founders on 1 Peter 2:18's specific command to obey *harsh* masters and on the household codes' demand for *fear* — a religiously loaded term in the LXX (phobos) that elsewhere is reserved for God. The deeper issue is the Bible's overall failure to condemn slavery as an institution. The household codes don't just permit slavery; they baptize the slave-master relationship into Christian theology by making slave-obedience a religious duty. The contradiction with Jesus' "call no man master" tradition is one of the canon's clearest indicators that the post-Pauline church traded the radical egalitarian gospel of earliest Christianity for institutional respectability. That is of course a judgment call on the evidence, but the textual evidence points in that direction.

contradictions.question: Do seed time and harvest ever cease?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 8:22, the Noahic covenant, declares that while the earth remains, "seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease." The Joseph cycle then narrates seven years of famine so severe that famine extends "in all lands" and "over all the face of the earth" (Genesis 41:54, 41:56, 45:11). The same book records a global agricultural failure that the same book had just promised would never occur.
contradictions.commentary: Read at face value, the contradiction is direct. The Genesis 8:22 covenant uses universal language — while the earth remains, seedtime and harvest will not cease. The Joseph narrative then describes a seven-year famine that the text repeatedly characterizes as global ("all lands," "all the face of the earth"). The Hebrew kol ha'aretz can be read locally ("all the land") or universally ("all the earth"), and apologists like Archer leverage that ambiguity to limit the famine to the Near East — Egypt, Canaan, and surrounding territories. That's textually plausible for the Joseph narrative; the Hebrew Bible regularly uses kol ha'aretz hyperbolically. The problem is that Genesis 41:57 says "all countries came into Egypt to Joseph for to buy corn," reinforcing the global framing. More importantly, even granting the localized reading, the question of "cessation" turns on whether seedtime and harvest in the affected region actually stopped. Genesis 41:54 says "the dearth was in all lands" and 41:56 says "the famine waxed sore in the land of Egypt" — meaning the agricultural cycle had functionally ceased for the duration of the famine in the regions described. So either (a) the Noahic covenant is universal and the Joseph famine is local, in which case the contradiction softens to a hyperbolic-language dispute, or (b) one of the two passages is using kol ha'aretz with a different scope than the other. Source-critically, Genesis 8:22 is generally assigned to J (the Yahwist) and the Joseph narrative is a complex composite (J/E with later P insertions). The contradiction is the result of the redactor folding originally independent traditions into a single narrative without flattening their internal tensions. Documentary Hypothesis predicts exactly this kind of doublet-by-juxtaposition.

contradictions.question: Which woman besought Jesus?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 15:22 identifies the woman who asked Jesus to exorcise her daughter as "a woman of Canaan" (gyne Chananaia). Mark 7:26, the source text Matthew is editing, identifies her as "Greek, a Syrophoenician by nation" (Hellenis, Syrophoinikissa to genei). The two designations describe different ethnic and political categories — Canaanite is a biblical-archaic Hebrew Bible term; Syrophoenician is a contemporary first-century Roman regional designation.
contradictions.commentary: This is a classic case of Matthean redaction of Mark, and the contradiction at the level of identification is genuine even if the underlying historical referent is the same person. Mark, writing first (most critical scholars c. 65-75 CE), calls her Greek (in religion/language) and Syrophoenician (in ethnicity/region) — accurate contemporary first-century terminology for someone from coastal Syria/Phoenicia. Matthew, writing later (c. 80-90 CE) and editing Mark for a more Jewish-Christian audience, replaces Syrophoenician with the archaic biblical term "Canaanite." The change is theologically purposeful. Matthew is reframing the encounter as a meeting between Jesus the Son of David and a representative of Israel's ancient enemies — the Canaanites whom Joshua failed to fully dispossess. The Canaanite designation reactivates Hebrew Bible categories that Mark's neutral ethnographic label does not. Apologists harmonize by noting that the two terms can refer to overlapping populations — Phoenicians were historically descendants of Canaanites, and the LXX sometimes uses Chanaan for the broader region. That's true. But the harmonization concedes the point: Matthew has deliberately replaced Mark's contemporary terminology with biblical-archaic terminology. The two designations aren't synonymous in first-century usage. Davies-Allison treat this as a clear example of Matthean redaction reshaping Mark's narrative for his own theological purposes. The contradiction isn't "Matthew made up a different woman" — it's that Matthew rewrote Mark's identification of the same woman to serve his own theological agenda, and the two designations don't match. That's not error per se; it's evidence that the Gospel writers are theologians, not transcribers.

contradictions.question: Where did Jesus ascend?
contradictions.summary: Acts 1:9-12 places the ascension on the Mount of Olives (Olivet), with the disciples returning to Jerusalem from there "a sabbath day's journey." Luke 24:50-51, written by the same author, places the ascension at Bethany, where Jesus led the disciples out and blessed them before being carried up to heaven. The two-volume Luke-Acts gives two different locations for the same event.
contradictions.commentary: This is a contradiction within a single author's two-volume work, which makes it especially interesting from a redaction-critical standpoint. Luke 24 compresses the entire post-resurrection sequence into what reads like a single Easter day — the appearance on the Emmaus road, the appearance to the eleven, and the ascension all seem to occur the same evening. Acts 1, by contrast, separates the ascension from the resurrection by forty days (1:3) and locates it on the Mount of Olives. Apologists like Marshall and Bock harmonize geographically by noting that Bethany sits on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, so the two locations can refer to roughly the same area — a real point of geography. They also harmonize chronologically by claiming Luke 24 telescopes the timeline without specifying a date. Both moves are textually possible but strained. Luke 24:50 specifies Bethany (eis Bethanian), not the Mount of Olives generally, and Acts 1:12 specifies the Mount of Olives as the return point, not Bethany. More importantly, Luke 24 reads as a complete narrative that does not anticipate a forty-day gap. The narrative friction is best explained as Luke writing his Gospel ending and then, when composing Acts later, rewriting the ascension to serve as the prologue/inciting incident of Acts. Critical scholarship has long recognized that Luke uses the ascension as the literary hinge between the two volumes, and the divergent details reflect his rewriting for different rhetorical purposes — closure for the Gospel, prologue for Acts. The geographical and chronological details get reshaped to fit each volume's narrative function.

contradictions.question: Where did Abraham depart to?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 12:5 reports that Abram took his household from Haran and "they went forth to go into the land of Canaan; and into the land of Canaan they came" — Abram knew his destination. Hebrews 11:8 reframes the same event as faith-departure: "he went out, not knowing whither he went." Genesis has Abram leaving with Canaan as a known target; Hebrews has him leaving in ignorance of the destination.
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction is genuine at the level of narrative reporting, but it's softer than the cleaner cases in this batch because Hebrews 11 is doing theological midrash on the Genesis narrative, not historical reporting. Genesis 12:1 records God's command "unto a land that I will shew thee" (el ha'aretz asher ar'ekka) — the destination is not specified in the divine command. But by 12:5, the narrator says they left specifically to go to Canaan, and they arrived. The Hebrew Bible doesn't tell us when or how Abram learned the destination was Canaan; the narrative gap allows the author of Hebrews to read Genesis 12:1's open-ended command as the operative moment, with Abram departing in faith before knowing the destination. Apologists harmonize by treating Hebrews 11:8 as commenting on the moment of departure (when the destination was unspecified) and Genesis 12:5 as describing the journey's outcome (when the destination had been disclosed en route). That's a plausible harmonization if you grant the chronological reading the apologist proposes. The harder problem is that the author of Hebrews is using Abraham as a faith exemplar in a theology of pilgrimage — he wants Abraham to stand for the Christian who departs his earthly home without knowing the heavenly destination. The theological agenda shapes the historical claim. Critical scholarship treats Hebrews 11 as a stylized hall-of-faith reread of biblical narrative for hortatory purposes, not as a transcript of what Genesis actually says. Read that way, the "contradiction" is really a difference in narrative purpose — Genesis tells us where Abraham went; Hebrews tells us what kind of faith departure means. Different aims, overlapping vocabulary, real tension at the propositional level.

contradictions.question: Did Abraham's children require interposition of Providence?
contradictions.summary: Romans 4:19 and Hebrews 11:12 both emphasize that Abraham's body was "as good as dead" and Sarah's womb was barren, so the birth of Isaac required miraculous divine intervention. Genesis 25:1-2 then reports that after Sarah's death, Abraham took Keturah as a wife and fathered six more sons — Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, Shuah — apparently without any supernatural assistance, despite being at least 137 years old (since Sarah died at 127 per Genesis 23:1, when Abraham was 137 per Genesis 17:17 / 25:7-10 reckoning).
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction here is more theological than narrative, and it has been a recognized puzzle since the rabbinic period. The Pauline-Hebrews argument depends on Abraham being reproductively dead to make Isaac's birth a paradigm of resurrection-faith. Romans 4:19 says Abraham "considered not his own body now dead, when he was about an hundred years old, neither yet the deadness of Sara's womb." The Keturah narrative in Genesis 25 — with six additional sons, plus the implication of grandchildren born during Abraham's lifetime — undermines that argument. If Abraham was reproductively functional enough to father six sons after Sarah's death (which occurred when he was 137), then his being "as good as dead" at 100 is exegetically suspect. Apologists like Calvin and Archer harmonize in two main ways. First, they argue that the Keturah marriage chronologically *preceded* Sarah's death — the narrative is non-sequential, and Keturah's children were born before or during the Isaac period, when Abraham was younger. The Genesis text does not support this; 25:1 reads "then again Abraham took a wife," placing Keturah after Sarah. Second, they argue that the Isaac birth involved Sarah's barrenness primarily, not just Abraham's age — so divine intervention was needed to restart Sarah's womb regardless of Abraham's continued fertility. That's textually defensible (Genesis 18:11 explicitly says Sarah was past childbearing). But Romans 4:19 explicitly names both — Abraham's deadness and Sarah's. The Keturah cycle puts pressure on the Pauline-Hebrews reading of Abraham as resurrection-typological. The simplest reading is that the Genesis traditions (which preserve older folkloric elements, including the Keturah line as ethnogenesis of the southern Arab tribes) and the Pauline-Hebrews theological reading are working with different agendas, and the later theological reading flattens the narrative complexity to make its rhetorical point.

contradictions.question: Was Canaan promised and given to Abraham and his seed?
contradictions.summary: Genesis 13:14-17 and Genesis 17:8 record God promising the land of Canaan to Abraham and his seed as an "everlasting possession" (achuzzat olam). Acts 7:5 and Hebrews 11:9, 13 directly state that Abraham received no inheritance in the land — "not so much as to set his foot on" — and that he and the patriarchs died in faith "not having received the promises." The Genesis promise of immediate and everlasting possession contradicts the New Testament's retrospective admission that the promise was never fulfilled to Abraham himself.
contradictions.commentary: This one is straightforward at the narrative level. Genesis 13:15 says "all the land which thou seest, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed for ever." Genesis 17:8 promises Canaan as an everlasting possession. Acts 7:5, Stephen's speech, flatly states that God "gave him none inheritance in it, no, not so much as to set his foot on." Hebrews 11:13 says "these all died in faith, not having received the promises." The New Testament texts know the contradiction exists and try to resolve it by spiritualizing the promise — Abraham's true inheritance is the heavenly Jerusalem (Hebrews 11:16), not the earthly land. That's a real harmonization strategy, but it concedes the historical-narrative point. Abraham did not, in his lifetime, possess Canaan. Apologists like Walton and Sailhamer harmonize by distinguishing between the promise (which was given to Abraham) and the fulfillment (which was promised to his descendants). Genesis 15:13-16 explicitly tells Abraham his seed will be afflicted four hundred years before returning to possess the land, so the deferred fulfillment is built into the narrative. That's textually correct — but it makes the "everlasting possession" language strange when applied to the patriarch himself, who never possessed it. Critical scholarship treats the Abrahamic land promise as a post-exilic theological retrojection — the J/E sources may preserve older tribal traditions, but the developed "everlasting possession" language likely reflects P's Second Temple theology of Israel's land claims being grounded in pre-conquest divine promise. Acts 7 and Hebrews 11, written in the post-70 CE diaspora when the land had been lost to Rome, deliberately spiritualize the promise to keep it operative when geopolitical fulfillment had failed. Same promise, two reading strategies — one literal-historical (Genesis), one spiritualized-eschatological (NT). The texts contradict at the propositional level; the NT resolves the contradiction by changing what "inheritance" means.

contradictions.question: How long should David's throne endure?
contradictions.summary: Psalm 89:35-37 records God's oath, sworn by his holiness, that David's seed shall endure forever and his throne be established as the sun and moon — a faithful witness in heaven. Eight verses later, the same psalm — Psalm 89:44 — says God has "made his glory to cease, and cast his throne down to the ground." The contradiction is internal to a single psalm: the eternal oath in v. 35-37 is followed by the report of the throne's destruction in v. 44.
contradictions.commentary: Psalm 89 is one of the most theologically explosive texts in the entire Psalter, precisely because the contradiction is internal and intentional. The psalm is a three-part composition. Verses 1-37 rehearse the Davidic covenant in maximalist terms, climaxing in God's unbreakable oath. Verses 38-45 then describe the catastrophic reversal — God has rejected, abhorred, broken, profaned, cast down. Verses 46-51 are the lament's prayer for restoration. The psalm is not contradicting itself by accident. The psalmist is *holding God accountable* for the contradiction. The structure is: here is what you swore; here is what has happened; how long, O Lord. Most critical scholars (Tate, Hossfeld-Zenger, Goldingay) date the psalm's final form to the exilic or early post-exilic period, when the Davidic dynasty had been destroyed and the eternal covenant looked like a broken promise. The psalm preserves the older Davidic theology in vv. 1-37 (likely pre-exilic court material) and then juxtaposes it with the exilic reality in vv. 38-45 to confront God with the breach. Apologists harmonize by appealing to messianic fulfillment — the throne was "cast down" for Israel but "restored" in Christ, the eternal Davidic king. That's the standard New Testament reading (Acts 2:30, Hebrews 1:8), but it's a theological resolution to a textual problem that the psalmist himself does not resolve. The psalm ends in unanswered lament. The contradiction is not just real — it's *deliberate*, used as rhetorical pressure on Yahweh. Treating it as a problem to be harmonized away misses the psalm's own theological move.

contradictions.question: Did Jesus lay down his life for friends or enemies?
contradictions.summary: John 15:13 and 10:11 describe Jesus laying down his life for his friends (philoi) and for the sheep — the in-group, the disciples, those who love him. Romans 5:10 says "when we were enemies (echthroi), we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son" — the death was for those who were hostile to God, not those who were loyal. The Johannine and Pauline atonement frameworks identify different beneficiaries of the same death.
contradictions.commentary: The contradiction is more theological-categorical than narrative, and it tracks a real divergence between Johannine and Pauline soteriology. In John's Gospel, the cross is presented within the discourse community of the disciples — the Farewell Discourse (John 13-17) frames the death as the supreme act of friendship-love. The Good Shepherd lays down his life for the sheep that belong to him; the friend lays down his life for his friends. Pauline soteriology in Romans 5:6-10 deploys the opposite framework: Christ died for the ungodly (asebon), for sinners, for enemies. The point Paul is making is that the death is unmerited and unilateral — it precedes the reconciliation, so the recipients were enemies at the time of the action. Apologists harmonize by noting that the two frameworks address different moments in the narrative. The Romans 5 "enemies" describes the soteriological starting point (before reconciliation); the John 15 "friends" describes the relational status of the disciples within the narrative (they are already Jesus' friends because they have followed him). On that reading, both can be true: Christ died for friends-who-were-formerly-enemies. That harmonization works at the systematic-theological level but flattens the distinct rhetorical aims of the two texts. John wants to elevate the cross as the supreme expression of in-group love — the disciples are friends, not slaves, because Jesus has revealed everything to them. Paul wants to magnify grace by emphasizing the moral asymmetry — Christ died for those who hated him. The two emphases serve different pastoral functions and resist easy synthesis. The deeper critical point is that John and Paul are working with different atonement theologies. Paul's reconciliation-of-enemies framework (Romans 5, 2 Corinthians 5:18-21) is forensic and substitutionary. John's friendship-laying-down-life framework is relational and revelatory. The texts contradict at the level of who-the-death-is-for because they're answering different soteriological questions.

contradictions.question: Was it lawful for the Jews to kill Jesus?
contradictions.summary: John 19:7 has the Jewish authorities declaring that under their own law, Jesus deserves death — "by our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God." John 18:31 has the same authorities saying to Pilate, "It is not lawful for us to put any man to death." Same group, same trial scene, two different answers about whether their law permits killing Jesus.
contradictions.commentary: The two verses live within the same trial narrative and reflect the historical-juridical complexity of capital cases under Roman occupation in the late Second Temple period. The apologist harmonization, which has substantial scholarly support, distinguishes between two claims: (1) under Jewish law, Jesus' alleged blasphemy was a capital offense (Leviticus 24:16), so John 19:7 reports the substantive verdict the Jewish authorities had reached; (2) under Roman occupation, the *ius gladii* — the right of capital execution — had been removed from the Sanhedrin and reserved for the Roman governor, so John 18:31 reports the procedural limitation. The two statements describe different categories: substantive law (yes, our law condemns him) and procedural authority (but we can't carry out the execution). That harmonization is historically defensible. Raymond Brown in *The Death of the Messiah* extensively documents the debate over whether the Sanhedrin retained capital jurisdiction in the late Second Temple period. The dominant scholarly view is that they did not — Rome had restricted capital cases to the prefect's court, which is exactly why the Jewish authorities need Pilate to ratify the execution. The tension in John is real but not necessarily contradictory at the legal level. Critically, however, John is using both statements rhetorically. The Fourth Gospel has a strong anti-Jewish polemic and is theologically invested in making the Jewish authorities responsible for Jesus' death while showing Pilate as the reluctant executioner. The two statements together work to assign maximum culpability to "the Jews" (John's hostile term for the religious authorities) while shifting procedural responsibility to Rome. The narrative contradiction at the surface dissolves into a coherent juridical picture, but only if you grant John's tendentious framing. The deeper critical issue isn't the legal mechanics but John's anti-Jewish polemic, which most contemporary scholarship (Reinhartz, Levine, Brown) treats as a serious historical and ethical problem.

contradictions.question: Are reward and punishment bestowed in this world?
contradictions.summary: Proverbs 11:31 declares that the righteous are recompensed in the earth — "much more the wicked and the sinner." The traditional Deuteronomic-Wisdom theology underwrites this: divine justice operates within the temporal frame of this life. Revelation 20:12, Matthew 16:27, and 2 Corinthians 5:10 relocate judgment to the eschaton — a final reckoning at the throne of judgment after death, when works are weighed and the book of life is opened. Same canonical question — when is justice administered — two different answers.
contradictions.commentary: This is one of the most theologically consequential contradictions in the Bible because it tracks the historical development of Jewish-Christian eschatology. The older Israelite worldview, embedded in the Deuteronomic theology and most of Proverbs, operated on a this-worldly justice model — keep covenant and you'll prosper; break covenant and you'll suffer. Sheol was a shadowy non-existence common to all, not a place of moral differentiation (cf. Ecclesiastes 9:5, 10; Job 3 — both cited in the SAB answer 1316). The post-exilic and Second Temple period developed apocalyptic eschatology — a final resurrection, divine judgment, eternal reward or punishment. Daniel 12:2 is the breakthrough text in the Hebrew Bible, dated by most critical scholars to the Maccabean crisis (c. 165 BCE), when the this-worldly justice model collapsed under the experience of righteous martyrs dying for covenant fidelity. The New Testament inherits and develops the apocalyptic eschatology fully. The contradiction the SAB highlights is historically accurate: the Bible contains two distinct theologies of divine justice — a pre-exilic immanent-justice model and a post-exilic transcendent-eschatological model. Apologists harmonize by claiming both are operative — God rewards some things in this life and reserves final judgment for the next. That's a coherent synthetic theology, and it's how most Christian traditions read the texts. But the synthesis flattens the historical development. The Wisdom tradition (Job, Ecclesiastes) is itself a sustained protest against the simple immanent-justice model — Job's friends recite the Proverbs 11:31 theology, and Job calls bullshit. Ecclesiastes 9 explicitly states that the same fate befalls the righteous and the wicked. The Bible contains an internal debate about whether this-worldly justice works, and the apocalyptic eschatology emerged precisely because the older theology had failed to comport with reality. That is not a contradiction to be harmonized — it is the canon recording its own theological evolution.

contradictions.question: Is annihilation or endless misery the portion of manking?
contradictions.summary: Job 3, Ecclesiastes 9:5, 10, and Ecclesiastes 3:19-20 articulate a thoroughgoing annihilationist anthropology — the dead know nothing, all go to dust, man has no preeminence above a beast, the grave is silence. Matthew 25:46, Revelation 20:10, 14:11, 20:15, and Daniel 12:2 articulate eternal conscious torment — everlasting punishment, smoke of torment rising forever, the lake of fire, awakening to everlasting shame. The Hebrew Bible's older anthropology and the apocalyptic-NT eschatology give incompatible answers about what happens after death.
contradictions.commentary: This is a sharper version of the previous contradiction (id 598) and tracks the same historical-theological development. The Hebrew Bible's mainstream anthropology — preserved most clearly in Job and Ecclesiastes — is what biblical scholars call a "holistic" view: human beings are animated bodies (nephesh chayyah), not embodied souls, and death is the cessation of life rather than the separation of soul from body. Ecclesiastes 9:5 ("the dead know not any thing") and 3:19-20 ("all are of the dust, and all turn to dust again") are not poetic exaggerations — they reflect the pre-apocalyptic Israelite consensus that death is real and final. Sheol, in this framework, is not hell; it's just the grave, the realm of non-being where everyone goes regardless of moral status. The transition to apocalyptic eternal-torment theology happens in the Second Temple period under multiple influences — Persian Zoroastrian dualism, Hellenistic body-soul dualism, and the theodicy crisis of the Maccabean martyrdoms (cf. 2 Maccabees 7, 1 Enoch). Daniel 12:2 is the first clear Hebrew Bible text positing differentiated post-mortem fates. The Synoptic Gospels and especially Revelation develop the doctrine fully — eternal conscious torment, the lake of fire, the worm that does not die. Apologists like John Walton and Edward Fudge propose either "progressive revelation" (early texts give partial truth, later texts give fuller truth) or, for Fudge specifically, *conditional immortality* / annihilationism — the wicked are destroyed, not eternally tormented, and texts like Job and Ecclesiastes preserve that older truth. The progressive-revelation move is theologically convenient but historically tendentious — it treats earlier Israelite anthropology as defective rather than as a distinct theological tradition. The annihilationist apologetic (Fudge, Stott in his later work) actually agrees with the SAB's reading that the canon contains conflicting eschatologies and chooses the older one. The contradiction is real, well-documented, and reflects the canon recording its own evolving anthropology of death.

contradictions.question: Is the Christian yoke easy?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 11:28-30 has Jesus offering rest to the weary — his yoke is easy (chrestos) and his burden is light (elaphron). John 16:33, 2 Timothy 3:12, and Hebrews 12:6, 8 give the opposite framing: in the world believers will have tribulation, all who live godly will suffer persecution, and those without chastisement are bastards rather than legitimate sons. The Matthean invitation and the persecution-discipleship theology of the rest of the New Testament give competing answers about whether following Christ is easy or hard.
contradictions.commentary: The tension is real but the harmonization is also strong here, so this is a softer contradiction than the cleaner cases in this batch. Matthew 11:28-30 is widely recognized as drawing on Wisdom traditions — Sirach 51:23-27 invites the unlearned to take up Wisdom's yoke and find rest, with closely parallel language. The Matthean Jesus is positioning himself as personified Wisdom, offering a yoke (a rabbinic metaphor for the discipline of Torah-study) that is paradoxically restful compared to the burdens the scribes and Pharisees impose (cf. Matt 23:4 — "they bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne"). The "easy" yoke is relative to the burden it replaces, not absolutely easy. Apologists like Carson and France harmonize on exactly this point: the Matthean yoke is easy in the sense that Christ's discipline is restful and life-giving, not in the sense that following Jesus is socially or physically painless. The persecution-discipleship texts (John 16:33, 2 Timothy 3:12, Hebrews 12:6) address the external opposition believers face, not the internal experience of the yoke. The two frames address different dimensions — the internal experience of devotion (easy, restful) and the external experience of persecution (hard, painful). That harmonization works reasonably well, and most critical commentators (Davies-Allison, Luz) note the wisdom-tradition background that frames the "easy yoke" relatively rather than absolutely. The genuine tension remaining is rhetorical rather than logical: Matthew 11:30's blanket statement ("my yoke is easy and my burden is light") doesn't include the qualifier the harmonization requires. Read at face value, alongside Jesus' own predictions of persecution and martyrdom for his followers (Matt 10:16-39), the saying does sit in tension with the broader NT picture. The contradiction softens with context but doesn't fully dissolve.
